one_line: A human-approved meeting scheduler where agents negotiate candidate times through shared WebMCP state.
what_it_does: Quorum lets humans and AI agents join a live scheduling session, vote on candidate times, counter-propose, rank slots, and record actions in a shared negotiation log; the organizer approves or locks the final time.
leverage_rationale: WebMCP is central to the claimed stateful, mixed human-agent negotiation: typed tools expose state, joining, voting, counter-proposals, and ranking with shared visibility. A general UI-driving agent could attempt this, but reliably chaining stateful actions and preserving precise shared state would be markedly harder.
leverage_evidence: About text describes seven page-registered WebMCP tools for reading state, joining, voting with reasons, counter-proposing, and ranking.
Frame sheet shows a dedicated WebMCP Tools panel with structured tool/schema content beside the live scheduling page.
Frames show candidate times, participants, negotiation log, and counter-proposals as shared product state.
execution_rationale: The packet presents a coherent scheduling workflow and the frame sheets show populated event creation followed by a roadmap review page with candidate ideas, participants, negotiation log, and counter-proposals. The core end-to-end agent action is claimed rather than directly demonstrated, and the later frames do not show a clear completed tool result.
execution_evidence: Video frames visibly show the populated Quorum interface and resulting Q3 roadmap review state.
Frame sheets show candidate items, participants, negotiation log, and counter-proposals.
Devpost packaging consistently presents the same scheduling concept and UI.
impact_rationale: Scheduling across people with conflicting constraints is a clear recurring problem, and agent participation plus human approval addresses coordination friction while retaining trust and control. The value is credible for teams and groups, though the packet does not independently establish broad real-world use.
impact_evidence: Pitch identifies negotiation over everyone's constraints as the scheduling problem.
Shared negotiation log and human organizer approval are visibly emphasized.
Candidate times, participant states, and counter-proposals are shown in the product frames.
creativity_rationale: The concept is a fresh synthesis of scheduling and multi-party agent negotiation, with human and agent participants acting in one shared session and an audit trail as part of the interaction model. The ambition is substantial for a hackathon, even though scheduling itself is an established category.
creativity_evidence: Pitch frames agents as equal participants who vote and counter-propose alongside humans.
The shared HUMAN/AGENT negotiation log and approval boundary create a distinctive interaction model.
Frame sheets show negotiation-oriented product surfaces rather than a simple scheduling form.
usability_note: The visible UI is organized around candidate times/items, participants, logs, and proposals; human approval is explicit. The workflow appears understandable, but direct usability testing is not included.
red_flags: No explicit tool-call result or completed success confirmation is visible in the frame sheets.
The prompt packet contains only one project packet despite requiring ten, so the review input appears incomplete.
standouts: Strong human-in-the-loop boundary: agents propose while the organizer approves or locks the decision.
Shared negotiation log makes agent actions inspectable.
WebMCP tools are presented as part of a stateful multi-party workflow rather than isolated UI buttons.
advance_reason: Advance based on a strong, coherent concept with visible product state and clear WebMCP leverage; stage-two observation should verify the claimed end-to-end agent negotiation.
